unit.title: Provide advice on retail beauty care products

summary: This unit teaches you to advise clients honestly on beauty care products they can use at home. You will learn to find out a client's needs with open questions, check for allergies and conditions, know your products (features and benefits, labels, hair, skin and sun care), present and demonstrate them hygienically, handle objections and complaints, complete a sale and look after stock, display and records, with respect for the client's rights and privacy.

blocks.p: Every salon service ends with a question: how will the client look after her hair, skin or nails at home? This unit teaches you to answer it. Good retail advice helps the client keep the results of her service, protects her from products that do not suit her, and builds the trust that brings her back.

This is **advice, not pressure**. A therapist who sells the wrong product, or makes a false promise, harms the client and the salon's name. So this unit is about **listening, product knowledge, honesty, safety and good record keeping** as much as about selling.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and two practical tasks. In one, your group role-plays retail consultations as therapist, client and observer, including a demonstration, an objection and a practice sale with a receipt. In the other, your group sets up a retail display, checks stock, writes product information cards and an aftercare leaflet, and counts the stock.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, use made-up names on forms. Photograph only hands, products and forms, never a person's face unless she agrees and the Centre allows it.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Why we advise, and good retail practice

blocks.h: Why a salon gives retail advice

ul: So the client can **care for her hair, skin or nails at home** and keep the result of her service longer.
To protect her from a product that does not suit her, or that she might misuse.
To build trust and repeat visits: a client who gets good advice returns and tells her friends.
To earn income for the salon. That is a result of good advice, never the reason to push a product.

blocks.p: Good advice is based on **the needs you find out in the consultation**, not on the product with the biggest profit, the one you like to use yourself, or the one with the loudest advertising. Examples: a client who has had a relaxer needs home care that keeps her relaxed hair moisturised and strong until her next visit; a client with an oily scalp needs gentle cleansing and light products.

head: Good practice
Poor practice
rows: Asks questions and listens
Talks all the time and interrupts
Recommends one or two products that match her needs and budget
Recommends the most costly or the one with the biggest profit
Tells the truth about what a product can do
Makes claims the maker does not make
Respects her decision, including 'no'
Keeps pressing, or makes her feel bad
Admits when she does not know, and finds out
Guesses, to avoid looking unsure
Keeps her details private
Discusses her purchases or conditions with others

blocks.h: Your own appearance and the shop floor

ul: Look neat, clean and professional; the client judges the products by you.
Know where each product is, what it costs and what it does.
Keep the retail area clean and tidy, and greet clients as they enter it.

head: On the label
What it tells you
rows: Product name and type
What it is for: shampoo, conditioner, moisturiser, sunscreen.
Manufacturer
The company that makes the product and writes its instructions: always follow them.
Ingredients list
Listed from the **largest amount first** to the smallest. Check it for allergens (for example nuts, fragrance, lanolin).
Directions for use
How much, how often, where to apply.
Warnings
Keep away from eyes; do a skin test; not for use on broken skin; flammable; keep out of reach of children.
Size
Written in millilitres (**ml**) or grams (g). A larger size usually costs less per ml.
Batch number and expiry date
Allow you to trace the product; the date after which it should not be sold or used.
Open-jar symbol (for example '12M')
Use the product within **12 months of opening**.
Claims such as 'non-comedogenic' or 'hypoallergenic'
Show what the maker says; they do not guarantee that no one will react.

blocks.p: A **feature** is a fact about the product: what it is or contains. A **benefit** is what that fact does for this client. Clients buy benefits.

head: Feature (the fact)
Benefit (what it does for her)
rows: Contains shea butter
Helps her dry hair feel softer and easier to comb.
Comes in a 250 ml bottle with a pump
Easy to use a small amount; lasts a few weeks.
Has an SPF of 30
Helps protect her skin from sunburn.
Is non-comedogenic
Unlikely to block her pores.
Is sulphate-free
Gentler on her coloured hair.

blocks.p: 'It comes in a nice bottle', 'it was made by a company that has been around for years' and 'it is on the shelf by the door' are not benefits to the client.

head: Skin type
Signs
Suits
rows: Normal
Smooth, balanced, small pores.
Gentle cleanser, light moisturiser, SPF.
Dry
Feels tight after washing; flaky, rough patches; fine lines.
Creamy cleanser, rich moisturiser; avoid drying products.
Oily
Shiny all over, large open pores, blackheads.
Foaming gel or light cleanser; oil-free, light moisturiser; clay mask.
Combination
Oily T-zone (forehead, nose and chin), normal or dry cheeks.
Different products for the two areas, or a balanced product.
Sensitive
Reddens easily; stings with products.
Mild, fragrance-free products; patch test.
Mature
Less firm; lines; often dry.
Rich, nourishing moisturiser, SPF, gentle exfoliation.

ul: **SPF** (sun protection factor) shows how well a sunscreen protects against sunburn (UVB). The higher the number, the more protection; none gives 100% protection.
Choose a **broad-spectrum** sunscreen that also protects against UVA, which ages the skin.
Apply plenty, about 15 minutes before going out; reapply every two hours, and after swimming or sweating.
Sunscreen is for every skin tone: dark skin can burn, age and develop dark patches too.
Sunscreen is for **every day**, even when it is cloudy, not only for the beach.

blocks.note: Jamaica's sun is strong all year. A client whose face is freshly cleansed after a facial, or whose skin has been waxed or exfoliated, burns more easily. Always include sun protection in aftercare advice.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Product
What it does
Who needs it
rows: Moisturising shampoo
Cleans gently without stripping oils.
Dry, relaxed or natural hair.
Clarifying or balancing shampoo
Removes build-up and excess oil.
Oily scalp; heavy product build-up (not for every wash).
Colour-care shampoo
Mild, helps slow fading.
Coloured hair.
Anti-dandruff shampoo
Controls flaking and itching.
Flaky, itchy scalp; follow the label.
Conditioner
Smooths the cuticle; makes hair easier to comb.
Everyone, on the lengths and ends.
Deep conditioning treatment
A richer treatment, used less often, as the label says.
Dry, damaged, relaxed or chemically treated hair.
Leave-in conditioner or cream
Moisture and slip between washes.
Dry, curly, coily or treated hair.
Heat protection spray or serum
Helps reduce heat damage from flat irons and blow dryers.
Anyone who uses heat at home.
Satin or silk bonnet, scarf or pillowcase
Reduces rubbing and moisture loss overnight.
Relaxed, natural, braided hair.

ul: **Cuticle oil** softens the cuticles and keeps the nails flexible; **hand cream** moisturises the skin. Both suit a client after a manicure.
A **top coat** applied every few days helps polish last; a gentle remover is kinder than a very strong one.
A foot file is for hard skin on the feet, not the hands.

blocks.p: A **safety data sheet** (SDS) is a sheet the supplier gives for a chemical product. It explains the hazards, safe use and storage, what to do in a spill, and first aid. Staff must know where the sheets are kept and read them for any product with hazards, such as aerosols, hair dyes and relaxers.

head: Type
What it is
Example
rows: Open question
Cannot be answered with yes or no; the client talks and you learn.
'How does your hair feel after washing?' 'What products do you use now?'
Closed question
Answered with yes or no; useful to confirm facts or check safety.
'Do you have any allergies?' 'Is your skin oily by midday?'

ul: Start with open questions to learn what she needs; use closed ones to check details.
**Listen carefully** and let her finish speaking. That finds her real needs and shows respect. A client who feels rushed or ignored will not trust your advice.
Use body language that shows interest: eye contact, a smile, a calm voice.
**Sum up** what she has told you to check you understood: 'So your hair feels dry at the ends and breaks when you comb it, is that right?'

head: Ask about
Why it matters
rows: What she uses now and how she likes it
Shows her routine and what has or has not worked.
Her hair or skin concerns, and what she wants
The core of her need.
Services she has had (relaxer, colour, facial, manicure)
Treated hair and skin have special needs.
Allergies, skin or scalp conditions, medicines, pregnancy
So you avoid products that could harm her.
Her routine, time and budget
So the advice is realistic.
Heat styling, swimming, sun, work
These all affect which products suit her.

ul: Ingredients such as **nut oils, fragrance, dyes, lanolin and preservatives** can cause allergies. If she tells you about an allergy, **read the ingredient list** before you suggest a product.
Do not recommend a product for **broken, weeping, infected or very irritated skin**, or a rash. That needs a doctor. Never offer a scrub or a strong product for it.
A skin or scalp condition you are not trained to deal with: say so and suggest a doctor or pharmacist.
Keep the product away from the eyes; for new products, suggest she tests a small area first.
Record any allergy and any reaction on her record card.

blocks.h: Skin tests for home colour and similar products

blocks.p: A client who buys a hair dye or other product that can cause an allergy should be told to do a **skin test** as the maker's instructions say. Many makers ask for it about **48 hours** before the colour is used, even for a product she has used before, because an allergy can develop at any time.

ul: She must read the maker's instructions fully and follow them exactly, and do a strand test if the maker asks.
Do not colour if there is any redness, itching or swelling at the test, or if the scalp is cut, sore or irritated.
Wear the gloves in the pack, work with fresh air, and keep colour away from the eyes; rinse at once with plenty of clean water if it gets in and get medical help.
Never mix it with another brand or leave it on longer than the instructions; throw away any mixed colour that is left.
Keep products out of reach of children.

blocks.note: The same rule applies in the salon: never sell a dye or relaxer for home use without explaining the skin test and the maker's directions.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Suggest **one or two** products that match what she told you, her allergies and her budget. Too many choices confuse her.
Link the product to something she said: 'You said your ends break when you comb them, so this leave-in will help.'

**Link selling** means suggesting a product that goes with the service she has just had: cuticle oil and hand cream after a manicure; a moisturising shampoo and a satin bonnet after a relaxer; sunscreen after a facial.
**Upselling** is offering a bigger size or a better version of the product she asked for. It is honest only if it truly suits her needs and budget.

blocks.h: Presenting a product: features, benefits, use, price

flow: Link it to her need
Give a feature
Turn it into a benefit for her
Show how to use it
Demonstrate it
Tell her the price clearly
Ask if she has questions; let her decide

head: Step
Example
rows: Link
'You said your hair feels dry and breaks when you comb it.'
Feature
'This leave-in contains shea butter and coconut oil.'
Benefit
'That helps your hair feel softer, easier to comb and less likely to break.'
How to use
'Use a small amount, about the size of a coin, through damp hair from the middle to the ends, as the label says.'
Price
'It is J$ 1,900 for the 250 ml bottle, and there is a smaller size at J$ 1,100.'
Close
'Would you like to try it? You can also take a sample.'

ul: Take a creamy product from a jar with a **clean spatula, used once**; never a finger.
Show a small amount of cream on the **back of her hand**, not on broken skin, a rash, a scratch or the delicate skin under the eye.
Check her allergy details first.
Keep tester lids on; keep testers clean and offer a fresh spatula to each client.
Wash or sanitise your hands before and after each demonstration.
A small free **sample** lets her try the product at home before she buys.

blocks.p: Tell the client how much to use, how often and where to apply it. This gets her the best result and keeps her safe. Follow the label: for example, if the label says a strong treatment is used **once a week**, tell her not to use it every day. Using more does not work faster and can harm the hair or skin. If she wants to share it with family, explain that products are chosen for one person's needs.

head: After a service
Suggest
rows: Relaxer
Mild moisturising shampoo; conditioner; deep treatment; leave-in; satin bonnet; heat protection for the flat iron.
Colour
Colour-care shampoo and conditioner; sun protection for the hair.
Facial
Cleanser, toner, moisturiser for her skin type; **a sunscreen every day**.
Manicure
Cuticle oil, hand cream, top coat, gentle remover.
Wax
No perfume or heat for 24 to 48 hours; gentle exfoliation after a few days; moisturiser; sunscreen.
Braids or locs
Light products; scalp spray; satin scarf; avoid heavy creams.

blocks.h: Home care for two different clients

head: Product
Dry, relaxed hair
Oily scalp
rows: Shampoo
Gentle moisturising shampoo
Balancing or clarifying shampoo, as often as the label says
Conditioner
Rich conditioner; weekly deep conditioning treatment, as the label says
Conditioner on the lengths and ends only, not on the scalp
Other
Light leave-in or oil for the ends; heat protection; satin bonnet at night
Avoid heavy oils and greases at the roots
Main idea
More moisture and protection
Gentle cleansing and lighter products

ul: Say only what the product can really do, as the maker's information shows.

**Never claim** that a beauty product treats a medical condition (for example, 'this cream will cure your eczema') or that it removes all wrinkles for good. It is untrue, and it can stop the client getting the medical care she needs.
Do not promise that a product works for every person or that it is 'guaranteed'.
Do not run down another product to sell yours.
Do not hide the price, or the tax; do not push a client to buy what she does not need.
If you do not know the answer, **say so** and find out, or suggest a doctor or pharmacist.

head: Honest
Not honest
rows: 'This moisturiser helps dry skin feel soft and smooth.'
'This will cure your eczema in a week.'
'Many clients with dry hair like this one. Let's see how your hair responds.'
'This works for everyone, guaranteed.'
'I don't know about that skin problem. I suggest you see a doctor.'
'Every cream will clear that up.'

ul: A client who buys a product has the right to accurate information, to a fair price shown clearly, and to a **receipt**.
Explain or display the salon's **returns or exchange policy** so clients know their rights before they buy.
Jamaica's **Consumer Affairs Commission** (CAC) helps consumers with their rights and complaints. Staff should be polite and fair, and should never try to stop a client from complaining to it.

blocks.p: An **objection** is a reason a client gives for not buying, such as the price. It is not a rejection of you. Stay calm and friendly, show you understand, and help her find a solution.

head: Objection
A good reply
rows: 'That shampoo is too expensive.'
'I understand. There is a smaller size that may suit, and one bottle lasts about a month.'
'I don't need it.'
'That's fine. May I note what we discussed on your card, in case you want it next time?'
'I'll think about it.'
'Of course. Here is a sample and the name of the product.'
'My friend uses a different one.'
'It may suit her hair. Yours is relaxed and dry, so this one is chosen for that.'
'I do not want anything today.'
Respect her choice; offer to note it on her card; do not keep pressing.

ul: Never argue, make her feel bad, say 'everyone buys it' or refuse to book her next appointment until she buys.
Offer choices: a smaller size, a lower-priced product that does a similar job, a sample, or noting it for next time.
The decision is hers. Thank her and give the same good service, so she feels respected and returns.

flow: Greet her politely and take her to a quiet place
Listen to the whole complaint without interrupting
Thank her and say you are sorry the product did not meet her needs
Ask questions: how she used it, how much, how often, what she expected
If there is a reaction, tell her to stop using it, and see a doctor if needed
Check the receipt and the returns policy; call the manager if you cannot decide
Offer a solution allowed by the policy: advice, exchange or refund
Record the complaint and the outcome and tell the manager

blocks.note: A calm, polite manner keeps the client's trust and the salon's good name. Do not tell her it cannot be the product, and do not give her a stronger product to stop an itch: stop using the product and see a doctor if the reaction is bad, spreading or near the eyes.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: If a client has a reaction

ul: Listen calmly and do not argue. Tell her to **stop using the product at once** and rinse the area with cool water.
If the reaction is bad, spreading or near the eyes, she should get medical help.
Tell the manager. Write the reaction, the product's name and its batch number on her record card, and follow the salon's returns and reporting policy.

sections.title: Completing the sale, payment and records

flow: Check the right product and size, an unbroken seal, and the expiry date
Tell her the total clearly
Take payment: cash or card
Count change back to her
Give her a receipt
Remind her how to use it and what to do if she has a reaction
Explain the returns policy
Bag the product and thank her
Record it on her card and update the stock sheet

ul: **GCT** is **General Consumption Tax**. If the salon is registered for GCT, it is charged on a sale at the **current rate**, as the law requires; the price shown to the client states whether it includes GCT.
Never leave GCT off for regular clients as a favour, add it only if asked for a receipt, or charge a rate that the therapist chooses.
Write the **receipt** clearly: date, products, price and GCT where it applies. Keep a copy for the salon.
Work out change carefully; count it back to the client.

blocks.note: Do not quote a GCT figure from memory; the rate can change. Use the salon's current rate and the price list the manager gives you.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Record on her card what she bought and any reaction, so the next stylist knows what she uses.
Client records are personal information. Under Jamaica's Data Protection Act they must be kept private and secure.
Do not show a client's card to anyone else. If a friend of a client asks what she bought, politely say you cannot share client details. Never post purchases or photos in a group chat.

blocks.p: **FIFO** means **first in, first out**: the older stock goes at the front and is sold first, and new stock is put behind it. This stops products from going out of date.

ul: Every product has an **expiry date**, the date after which it should not be sold or used. Check it when stock comes in and again regularly.
The **open-jar symbol** with a number (for example '12M') means use the product within 12 months of opening.

Take any out-of-date, damaged or leaking product off the shelf, set it aside in a labelled box, and follow the salon's procedure. Never sell it at half price without saying why, hide it behind newer stock, or mix it with new stock.
A broken seal means the product may have been tampered with or contaminated: do not sell it.
Store products in a **cool, dry place away from direct sunlight and heat**. Jamaica's heat can spoil creams, separate lotions and weaken active ingredients.
Keep **aerosols** (hairspray) away from heat, flames, the sun and hot tools.
Do not store stock on the floor near drains, in the front window, next to the dryer hood or on a water heater.
Keep products in their original, labelled containers; keep heavy items low and lids closed.

head: Good
Poor
rows: Clean shelves, tidy rows, labels facing out
Dusty shelves with products in no order
A clear price on every product
No prices, so clients must ask
Products grouped by type: hair, skin, nails, sun care
Everything mixed together
Testers clean, with lids on, and clean spatulas offered
Open testers left in the sun
Older stock at the front
Damaged boxes at the front to sell first
Out of direct sunlight, away from heat
In a sunny window

blocks.p: A clear **price label** on every product lets clients see the cost and choose freely.

blocks.h: Setting up and looking after a display

flow: Take everything off the shelves
Clean the shelves with a suitable cleaner, wearing gloves
Check each product for expiry date, open-jar symbol, broken seals and damage
Set problem items aside in a labelled box and list them on the stock sheet
Arrange products by group, older stock in front, labels facing out
Add a clear price label to each
Count stock and fill in the stock sheet
Dust and tidy daily; refill from the stock room

ul: Count the retail stock regularly. It shows what is selling and when to reorder.
Record what is sold, what comes in, and any problem items on the stock sheet.
Report low stock to the manager before it runs out.

blocks.h: Health and safety in the retail area

ul: A bottle breaks or oil spills on the floor: warn people, clean it up, and dry the floor. For broken glass, do not use bare hands: sweep it up and wrap it before binning it.
A product in the client's eye: rinse at once with plenty of clean, cool water and get medical help if it stays sore.
Use a proper step stool for high shelves; never climb on chairs or trolleys.
Lift heavy boxes with bent knees and a straight back, or ask for help.
Use shelf cleaner as the label says, with gloves and fresh air; never mix cleaning products.
I can explain why a salon gives retail advice and base my advice on the client's needs.
I can read a label: ingredients, directions, warnings, size, batch, expiry date and the open-jar symbol.
I can tell a feature from a benefit and present a product using both.
I can match products to skin types, hair types and sun care needs.
I can use open questions, listen, and sum up what the client needs.
I can check for allergies and conditions, and refer a client to a doctor when needed.
I can explain the skin test for home hair colour and give safety advice.
I can recommend one or two suitable products and use link selling honestly.
I can demonstrate a product hygienically with a clean spatula on the back of the hand.
I can give clear instructions for use and aftercare advice.
I can give honest advice and never make medical claims or false promises.
I can explain consumers' rights, receipts and the returns policy.
I can handle an objection and a complaint politely, and deal with a reaction.
I can complete a sale, including GCT at the current rate and a receipt.
I can look after stock with FIFO, check expiry dates, store products safely, build a clean display and keep client records private.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step. For example: 'I use a clean spatula once, so that germs from my fingers or another client do not get into the jar.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Retail product
A product sold to clients to use at home.
Manufacturer
The company that makes a product and writes its instructions.
Feature
A fact about what a product is or contains.
Benefit
What the feature does for the client.
Open question
A question that cannot be answered with yes or no.
Closed question
A question answered with yes or no.
Link selling
Suggesting a product that goes with a service.
Upselling
Offering a bigger size or better version of what she asked for.
Sample
A small free amount of product to try at home.
Objection
A reason a client gives for not buying, such as price.
Aftercare
Advice on caring for hair or skin at home after a service.
SPF
Sun protection factor: how well a sunscreen protects against sunburn.
Combination skin
An oily T-zone with normal or dry cheeks.
Non-comedogenic
Made so that it is unlikely to block pores.
Exfoliation
Removing dead skin cells from the surface.
Safety data sheet (SDS)
The supplier's sheet on a product's hazards, safe use, storage and first aid.
Skin test
A small test on the skin, usually about 48 hours before, to check for allergy.
Batch number
A code that identifies a product's production batch.
Expiry date
The date after which a product should not be sold or used.
Open-jar symbol
A pot symbol with a number such as 12M: use within that many months of opening.
FIFO
First in, first out: sell older stock first.
GCT
General Consumption Tax, charged at the current rate if the salon is registered.
Receipt
A written record of a sale given to the client.
Returns policy
The salon's rules for returns and exchanges.
Consumer Affairs Commission
The Jamaican body that helps consumers with their rights and complaints.
Stock sheet
The record of stock counted, sold, received and set aside.
Record card
The client's record of consultation, advice, purchases and reactions.
Data Protection Act
The Jamaican law that protects personal information.

c1.title: A relaxer client in Old Harbour
c1.text: Sherene Brown, 28, has just had a relaxer at a salon in Old Harbour. She uses a flat iron most mornings and says her ends break when she combs them. Trainee Kimani wants to sell her the most expensive range on the shelf because it has a bigger profit for the salon. Sherene says money is tight this month.

c2.title: A skin complaint at the counter in Savanna-la-Mar
c2.text: In a salon in Savanna-la-Mar, Mrs. Eunice Dixon, 44, asks trainee Camille for a strong scrub for the red, cracked, weeping patches on her cheeks. A different client, Latoya, returns a face cream she bought last week: her skin itches and is red where she used it. Latoya says she is allergic to nuts, and the cream's label lists almond oil.

c3.title: Home hair colour in Montego Bay
c3.text: Marcia Allen, 36, wants to buy a box of permanent hair colour at a salon in Montego Bay. She says she has used a different brand for years with no problem and wants to colour her hair tomorrow. The box says to do a skin test about 48 hours before.

c4.title: A price objection in Kingston
c4.text: A client, Rochelle Campbell, likes a vitamin serum at a salon in Kingston but says it costs too much. Trainee Dwayne tells her 'you cannot get beautiful skin without spending more'. When she says she does not want anything today, he says he will not book her next appointment until she buys something.

c5.title: Stock check in the training salon in Mandeville
c5.text: In the Centre's retail area in Mandeville, trainees clean the shelves and check the stock. They find a jar with an open-pot symbol and '12M' that was opened 14 months ago, a bottle of hairspray on the window shelf in the afternoon sun, and a cracked bottle of hair oil leaking onto the floor. Adrian wants to put the oldest stock at the back, behind newer bottles.

questions.q: What should Kimani base his recommendation to Sherene on?
o: The needs and budget she described in the consultation
The range that earns the salon the biggest profit
The product he uses on his own hair at home
The range with the brightest packaging on the shelf
questions.why: Good retail advice is built on the client's needs, which Kimani finds out by asking and listening, together with her budget. Profit, personal taste and packaging are not reasons to recommend a product.

questions.q: Which product does Sherene most need to protect her hair from her flat iron?
o: A clarifying shampoo for use at every wash
A heat protection spray or serum
A strong protein hair mask every day
A hair dye in a darker shade
questions.why: Heat from a flat iron damages the hair, and a heat protection product helps reduce that damage. Her relaxed hair also needs moisture, so a gentle moisturising routine is part of the advice.

questions.q: Which question is the best open question to start with?
o: Do you want to try a new shampoo today?
Is your hair relaxed or is it natural?
How does your hair feel after washing?
Have you ever used a conditioner before?
questions.why: An open question cannot be answered with yes or no, so Sherene has to describe her hair and the therapist learns her real needs. The others are closed questions, or push her towards buying.

questions.q: Kimani describes a leave-in by saying 'it contains shea butter and coconut oil'. What is that?
o: A benefit
An objection
A feature
A contraindication
questions.why: A feature is a fact about what the product is or contains. The benefit is what that fact does for the client, for example helping her dry hair feel softer and easier to comb.

questions.q: What should Camille do about Mrs. Dixon's red, weeping patches?
o: Sell her the scrub and tell her to use it gently
Sell a milder scrub and tell her to use it twice a day
Give a free sample to try on the patches tonight
Not sell the scrub; advise her to see a doctor
questions.why: Red, weeping, broken skin needs medical care, and a scrub could make it worse. A therapist never sells a product for such a condition, and does not name a disease.

questions.q: What should Camille do first when Latoya returns the cream?
o: Tell her it cannot be the cream and ask for proof
Tell her to stop using it, listen and tell the manager
Give her a stronger cream to stop the itching now
Offer her the same cream in a larger size
questions.why: Listen calmly, tell her to stop using the product, rinse the area, and tell the manager so the complaint and the product's batch can be recorded. A stronger or larger cream would make matters worse.

questions.q: What went wrong when the cream was sold to Latoya?
o: The price was not shown clearly on the shelf
The cream had not been kept in a cool place
Nobody checked the ingredient list against her nut allergy
She was not told to test it only on the back of her hand
questions.why: Nut oils such as almond oil can cause allergic reactions. When a client reports an allergy, the therapist reads the ingredient list before suggesting any product.

questions.q: Which record should be made of Latoya's complaint?
o: Her reaction, the product and batch, and the outcome
Only the price and the date on a sticky note
Nothing, since she has already returned the cream
A note in the receptionist's own phone
questions.why: The reaction, the product's name and batch, and what was done are written on her record card and in the complaints book, and the manager is told, so the team can learn from it.

questions.q: What should the therapist tell Marcia about the skin test?
o: It is not needed, as she has used hair colour for many years
She should do it as the maker says, even if she has used colour
She should do it only if her scalp feels itchy or sore
She should do it on her eyelid, 5 minutes before she colours
questions.why: An allergy can develop at any time, so the maker's skin test (often about 48 hours before) is done every time. It is never done on the eyelid.

questions.q: Marcia is keen to colour tomorrow. What is the right advice?
o: Skip the test and colour, since it only takes a few minutes
Mix the colour with her old brand to make it gentler
Colour as planned, but leave it on a little longer
Do the skin test now and wait the time the maker states
questions.why: Colour is used only after the skin test has been read as negative, and only as the instructions say. She must not mix brands or leave the colour on longer than the instructions state.

questions.q: Which safety advice should the therapist give about using the colour at home?
o: Wear the pack's gloves, keep colour from the eyes, ventilate
Use a metal bowl and spoon so the colour mixes well and evenly
Keep the leftover mixed colour in a bottle for the next time she colours
Rinse with very hot water, so the colour sets faster
questions.why: She should wear the pack's gloves, work with fresh air, keep colour away from her eyes and throw away any mixed colour left over. Mixed colour cannot be kept.

questions.q: Which reply to Rochelle's price objection is best?
o: Offer a smaller size or a sample, and respect her choice
Tell her cheaper serums are not safe for skin
Say that everyone else buys it at this price
Tell her she should not come back until she can afford it
questions.why: Respond calmly with options such as a smaller size, a cheaper product that does a similar job, or a sample, then let her decide. Running down other products or shaming her loses her trust.

questions.q: What is wrong with Dwayne's refusal to book Rochelle's next appointment?
o: Nothing, since a salon should only serve clients who buy
It pressures her; the decision is hers to make
It is correct only if she is a regular client
He should refuse on the day, but book later by phone
questions.why: A client has the right to say no. Pressuring her, or withholding service until she buys, is poor practice that loses her trust and may lead her to complain.

questions.q: Rochelle asks if the serum will remove all her wrinkles. What is the honest reply?
o: Yes, it removes all wrinkles for good in a month
It may help skin look smoother, but not remove every wrinkle
Yes, if she uses double the amount every day
It does the same for everyone, and it is guaranteed
questions.why: Only claim what the maker's information supports. Promises such as removing all wrinkles for good, or working for everyone, are false and can break consumer law.

questions.q: What should be done with the jar opened 14 months ago, with '12M' on it?
o: Sell it at half price without telling the buyer why
Put it at the back of the shelf behind the newer stock
Take it off the shelf and follow salon procedure
Mix its contents with new stock of the same product
questions.why: The open-jar symbol means use within 12 months of opening. A product past that time is taken off the shelf and dealt with as the salon's procedure says; it is not sold, hidden or mixed with new stock.

questions.q: What should happen to the hairspray on the window shelf?
o: It should stay there so clients can see it from outside
It should move next to the hot tools so it is handy
It should move to the back shelf over the water heater
It should move to a cool place away from sun, heat and flames
questions.why: Aerosols are kept away from heat, flames and direct sun, as the label says; a hot can may burst. Do not store them near hot tools or a water heater.

questions.q: What should be done first about the cracked bottle leaking oil onto the floor?
o: Mop it into the drain with plenty of hot water
Leave it for the night cleaner and carry on
Warn people, clean it up and dry the floor
Cover it with a towel and keep selling
questions.why: An oil spill is a slipping hazard: warn people (a sign), clean it up, and dry the floor. Then record the damaged item.

questions.q: Why is Adrian wrong to put the oldest stock at the back?
o: Older stock goes in front, to sell first (FIFO)
Stock should be sorted by price, not by age
New stock should always be sold before old stock
The oldest stock should be given away to staff
questions.why: FIFO means first in, first out: the oldest stock goes at the front and sells first, so products do not go out of date on the shelf.

questions.q: A client asks what 250 ml means on a shampoo bottle. What do you tell her?
o: The bottle holds 250 millilitres of shampoo
The shampoo is for hair of 250 mm length or longer
The shampoo lasts 250 days if used daily
The bottle must be used within 250 days of opening
questions.why: ml stands for millilitre, a unit of volume. It tells her how much product is in the bottle, which she can use to compare the price of different sizes.

questions.q: A client's friend asks you to tell her what the client bought last month. What should you do?
o: Tell her, if the friend buys something too
Show her the client's record card
Say you cannot share client details
Post the list in the staff group chat
questions.why: Client records are personal information, kept private under the Data Protection Act. Politely say you cannot share them with anyone who does not need them.
